title: GitHub - chipload/chipload: Open Source 2.5D CAM software for CNC routing, V-carving and 3D-Relief engraving
excerpt: Open Source 2.5D CAM software for CNC routing, V-carving and 3D-Relief engraving - chipload/chipload
content_html:
2.5D CAM for CNC routers and mills: drawings in (DXF, SVG or drawn in the app), checked G-code out. Free software for Linux, Windows and macOS, written in Rust.

User guide · Download

The relief above: 3DBenchy by Creative Tools (CC0), 150 mm wide and 10 mm deep, roughed with a 6 mm end mill and finished with a 2 mm ball nose.

Testers with real machines wanted. Chipload's programs pass its own checker, and they cut wood on a GRBL router (a Shapeoko), but they haven't yet run on LinuxCNC or Mach3/4, nor in inches. If you have a CNC router or mill, please try it, starting with an air cut, and tell us how it went.

Highlights

  • Checked G-code, always. An independent checker reads every program before it is written: machine limits, rapids through the stock, retracts, arcs, feeds.
  • Operations: profile (spiral, tabs, finishing pass, onion skin, dogbones), pocket (islands, spiral rings, rest passes, finishing pass, helical entry), V-carve, prism (raised letters with a ridge), chamfer, follow path, flute (grooves that ramp in and out), fill patterns (lines, cross-hatch, rings, waves, fluted strokes), moulding (a profile swept along a path), holes (drilled or bored), surfacing and relief.
  • Reliefs: carve a 3D model (STL), a depth-map picture or a logo inflated into rounded shapes, from the top with a ball nose; a rim that ramps up to the surface, roughing in levels and a smoothing pass, all set up in one wizard.
  • See it before you cut: a material-removal simulation in 3D, playback, cycle time, chip load and a setup sheet for the operator.
  • Drawings: draw and edit in the app (snapping, typed values, offset, fillet, trim, union and subtract, arrays, construction lines, and the Compass: one handle to move, turn, copy and array), or bring in several DXFs and SVGs, text in built-in fonts and traced pictures, mixed in one project; a new version of a DXF keeps the operations, and the drawing exports as a DXF.
  • A sheet of parts: several parts with their own operations, each placed again as instances that can be moved, turned and mirrored; export the whole sheet or one part.
  • Nesting: what the tools really cut, packed onto the board as a compact block or keeping a strip free, many orders and turns tried; what doesn't fit onto more boards.
  • Setups: cut parts from several boards, each with its own stock and work zero, a part's thickness picking its board; two-sided work with the back turned over and located by dowel pins.
  • The work zero where you want it: a stock corner, its centre, the drawing origin or any point, dragged in the view.
  • Your tools, materials and machines in a library, with your own feeds per tool and material, copied into each project, so it cuts the same on any computer.
  • Any controller: GRBL, LinuxCNC and Mach3/4 posts with arcs, in mm or inches. A post is a template and a small config, easy to copy and change.
  • Scriptable: every feature on the command line, --json everywhere, and chipload mcp for AI assistants.
  • In seven languages: English, German, French, Spanish, Italian, Swedish and Russian (translations waiting for review by machinists: corrections welcome).
  • No account, no network, no install. Your files stay on your computer.

Safety warning

CNC machines are dangerous. A wrong program can break tools, throw parts, damage the machine and injure people. The checker only catches the mistakes it knows about: it can't see your stock, clamps, tool or machine.

Check every program yourself before you run it: look at it in a G-code viewer (such as NC Viewer or CAMotics), do an air cut with a hand on the stop button, and never leave a running machine. Chipload comes with no warranty (GPL-3.0, sections 15 and 16).

Testing on your machine

Every report helps, "it worked" too. Start with a shallow cut in scrap, after an air cut. Useful to test: your controller and sender, arcs and helices, holes, several tools, inch G-code, and whether the work zero and depths match the setup sheet.

Open an issue with the machine, controller and sender, the Chipload version and post, the project file and G-code, and what happened. Problems found this way become test cases.

Download

Releases have the app as one file, chipload-X.Y.Z-…, for Linux (AppImage) and Windows (.exe), x86_64 and ARM64, and macOS (universal .dmg). The command line for scripts is in the chipload-cli-X.Y.Z-… archives, and the user guide to read offline in chipload-guide-X.Y.Z.zip.

Build from source

With Rust 1.95 or newer (rustup):

cargo run --release -p chipload-gui                      # the app
cargo run --release -p chipload-cli -- --help            # the command line
cargo test --workspace                                   # the tests

chipload new -o part.chipload --thickness 12     # an empty project to draw in
chipload shape add part.chipload rectangle --center 0,0 --length 160 --width 100
chipload op add part.chipload profile --shapes 1 --through
chipload import plate.dxf -o plate.chipload      # or a project from a DXF
chipload run part.chipload -o part.nc            # checked G-code and a setup sheet
chipload check part.nc --job part.chipload       # the checker on any G-code

Everything else is in the user guide. Contributors: CONTRIBUTING.md, docs/architecture.md for an overview, and CLAUDE.md for the rules.

Chipload is free software: you can redistribute it and/or modify it under the terms of the GNU General Public License as published by the Free Software Foundation, either version 3 of the License, or (at your option) any later version. See LICENSE.

What you make with Chipload is yours. The licence covers Chipload itself, not what you make with it: your drawings, projects, G-code and parts are yours to use and sell. Text cut in the built-in fonts (GNU FreeFont) is free of it too, by the fonts' own exception.
